articles.title: Trump says $5,000 ‘dividend’ would be ‘easy’ to fund if Republicans win midterms
articles.summary: US News: US president Donald Trump has renewed his promise to give every adult American a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress in Novemb.
articles.body: US president Donald Trump has renewed his promise to give every adult American a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress in November’s midterm elections, arguing that the government would have enough revenue to fund the payment.Speaking to reporters in Ireland on Sunday, where he was attending a golf tournament at his club in Doonbeg, Trump said the payments could be managed if Republicans win.“I don't know but it's easy if the Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we're taking in so much money,” Trump said when asked whether Congress would need to approve the payments.Trump first unveiled the proposal at a Republican Party convention in Dallas last week, linking the promised payout to what he described as trillions of dollars coming into the country.On Friday, he reiterated the pledge, saying, “If we win the midterms, we will provide Trump dividend, $5,000 for every adult citizen in our country. And we can do that because our country has never done better. We're taking in trillions, trillions of dollars. There's never been any country, not even close, that's come anywhere near. So it's $5,000 for every adult. We love our adults. It's about time we take care of our adults.”Trump also tied the proposal to his tax-cut agenda, saying: “We will make all Trump tax cuts. We're going to take those beautiful tax cuts. We're going to make them permanent because the Democrats want to end all those tax cuts. They want you to pay much higher taxes.”The proposed payment would carry a price tag of about $1.2 trillion, based on the US Census Bureau estimate of roughly 245 million adult US citizens, according to PBS. Trump has not provided details on how the payments would be funded.Trump had also promised $2,000 tariff dividend checks last November, but those payments never went out. The Tax Foundation had estimated tariff revenue would not cover the earlier $280–607 billion cost.Trump's proposal now faces questions over congressional approval, financing and its wider fiscal implications as the November midterms draw closer.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meghan shares first glimpse of family life after return to UK
articles.summary: It's the first time the Duchess of Sussex had posted her family on her Instagram grid since they return to the UK last month.
articles.body:
The Duchess of Sussex has shared a glimpse of family life in footage posted to Instagram following their return to the UK.

The 34-second clip, which features Wham!'s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go, begins with Meghan, along with her husband Prince Harry, walking along a country path as she turns and says "come on, you".

UK flag and heart emojis are shown throughout the video, which also shows their son Archie running towards deer as their daughter Lilibet rides her bike.

Another clip sees Harry fishing with the children as their dog walks alongside the water.

It's the first time the Duchess has posted her family on her Instagram grid since the Sussexes returned from from the US after living in California.

It is unclear when, or where, the footage posted on Sunday afternoon was taken , but one clip shows a pair of wellington boots walking on the spot in a puddle and the children also appear to be in waterproof boots as they head toward the deer.

The post offers a rare glimpse into the lives of seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet.

Whereas Meghan does occasionally show the couple's children on social media, their faces are often obscured as they are photgraphed from behind or their faces are hidden by their parents.

Alongside all the outside footage, there is also a moment showing a child's feet in front of an open fire.

Last month, a spokesman for the Sussexes would not confirm the family's arrival in the UK, but did say they were bringing their dogs, Mia and Pula,with them.

The couple adopted a black Labrador retriever several years ago, which is seen several times in the clip.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals and began a new life in the US in 2020.

They have not returned to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals.

It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area, and Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in a school.

Last week, a spokesperson for both the Duke and Duchess said the couple were surprised by a letter send by the Prince's father, King Charles III, clarifying they would remain non-working royals.

The spokesperson said the couple "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".

The letter, sent on behalf of the King, spelt out the non-working royal status of Prince Harry and Meghan.

They will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness", and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.

Mike Flood (Neb.) said Sunday he supports providing the Pentagon with more funding amid the Iran war over passing legislation to implement President Trump’s $5,000 dividend proposal. “First thing, I think we need to see the proposal, but the priority, in my opinion right now, should be funding our troops and replenishing our…
articles.body:
GOP Rep. Mike Flood (Neb.) said Sunday he supports providing the Pentagon with more funding amid the Iran war over passing legislation to implement President Trump’s $5,000 dividend proposal .

“First thing, I think we need to see the proposal, but the priority, in my opinion right now, should be funding our troops and replenishing our munitions before we do anything,” Flood told host Chris Stirewalt on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

Trump on Wednesday pledged to provide every American adult with $5,000 if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate in November. There are roughly 270 million adults in the U.S.

The president has previously promised to provide Americans with tariff rebate checks, and his administration reallocated funding from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to give U.S. service members a $1,776 dividend last holiday season.

“Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas.

Multiple GOP lawmakers have pushed back on the proposal , saying it would lead to inflation . Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) called the idea a “ socialist vote-buying scheme ” on Thursday.

But Flood, a member of the House Financial Services Committee, took a different tact. The Nebraska Republican said Trump promising to send American adults a $5,000 dividend is “no different than promising tax cuts,” which the GOP implemented last year in the form of the One Big Beautiful Bill.

“If that also gets the economy to where we need it to go and increases our growth, our GDP [gross domestic product], then let’s look at it. I think the priority needs to be the military,” Flood told Stirewalt, referring to the impacts of the president’s dividend.

The Trump administration sought $67.1 billion in additional defense funding from Congress earlier this summer, a request that included $17.3 billion in operational costs and $21 billion for munitions.

Since the administration asked for the funding, the Iran war has marched on into its seventh month — further depleting the Pentagon’s stockpiles of missile interceptors.

articles.title: South Korea eyes nuclear submarines to counter North Korea, protect key Indo-Pacific sea lanes
articles.summary: International News: South Korea's planned nuclear-powered submarine fleet could eventually operate beyond the Korean Peninsula, with military experts arguing that the ves.
articles.body: South Korea's planned nuclear-powered submarine fleet could eventually operate beyond the Korean Peninsula, with military experts arguing that the vessels could protect vital sea lanes, strengthen undersea cooperation with the United States and play a broader role in the Indo-Pacific.The debate over the programme has increasingly shifted from whether Seoul needs nuclear-powered submarines to how and where they should be deployed. While countering North Korea's growing submarine and nuclear capabilities is expected to remain their primary mission, experts say their long underwater endurance and ability to conduct extended operations could allow them to undertake missions across the wider Indo-Pacific.The assessments come after a senior US Navy official questioned whether South Korea had a clear security rationale and concept of operations for the costly vessels, particularly if they were intended to operate mainly in waters close to the Korean Peninsula.Moon Keun-sik, a submarine expert who formerly headed the nuclear-powered submarine project team at Navy Headquarters and is now a professor at the Graduate School of Public Policy at Hanyang University in Seoul, said such an assessment overlooks one of the key advantages of nuclear-powered submarines.“Diesel-powered submarines have to come close to the surface several times a day to recharge their batteries, exposing themselves in the process,” Moon told The Korea Times. “A nuclear-powered submarine can remain submerged for a long time and surface only when necessary.”North Korea remains primary targetMoon said the ability to remain submerged for extended periods would be critical for continuously tracking North Korean submarines capable of carrying nuclear weapons.North Korea is also pursuing a nuclear-powered submarine, which could make it increasingly difficult for conventional diesel-electric submarines to match its endurance and speed.South Korea's proposed nuclear-powered submarines would therefore give the country's navy a greater ability to monitor and respond to North Korean underwater threats without the operational limitations faced by conventionally powered submarines.Moon, however, argued that Seoul should not restrict the future fleet's mission to the Korean Peninsula.He pointed to South Korea's heavy dependence on maritime trade and sea lanes carrying energy supplies from the Middle East through the Indian Ocean and the Strait of Malacca.In a contingency involving the Strait of Hormuz or other strategically important waterways, nuclear-powered submarines could potentially be deployed for long-range missions, he said.Wider Indo-Pacific roleMoon has also argued that the submarines could protect South Korea's sea lines of communication while allowing Seoul to undertake more reciprocal undersea cooperation with the US Navy across the Indo-Pacific.Such a role could reduce South Korea's dependence on US nuclear-powered submarines for certain missions while giving Washington an additional capable undersea partner in the region.Cheng Seong-chang, vice president of the Sejong Institute, similarly said the primary mission of the vessels should be deterring North Korea's nuclear-powered submarines, but their strategic impact could extend beyond the peninsula.“The primary objective is, of course, to counter North Korean nuclear-powered submarines,” Cheong said. “But secondarily, they could help maintain the balance of power in Northeast Asia and take the South Korea-U.S. alliance to another level.”Cheong said a South Korean nuclear-powered submarine fleet would inevitably factor into China's strategic calculations and could ultimately support US strategy in the Indo-Pacific.The potential expansion of the submarines' role comes as Washington continues to examine the strategic implications of Seoul's plans.Adm. Daryl Caudle, the US chief of naval operations, said last week that South Korea needs a “valid reason” for acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and should have a clear operational concept for the vessels. He had previously suggested that Seoul might not need nuclear-powered submarines if it intended to operate them only in nearby waters.The comments have added to the debate over whether South Korea's planned fleet should be designed primarily as a peninsula-focused deterrent or as a force capable of undertaking longer-range Indo-Pacific missions.Seoul moves ahead with programmeDespite the questions in Washington, South Korea is moving forward with its nuclear-powered submarine programme.President Lee Jae Myung has described the project as a potential symbol of a stronger and more constructive South Korea-US alliance and has called for faster progress.The Ministry of National Defense aims to launch the first submarine in the mid-2030s and commission it in the late 2030s.The ministry says the vessel's prolonged underwater endurance and high mobility would make it a key asset against North Korea's submarine-launched nuclear and missile threats.The government has allocated 100 billion won ($74.4 million) in next year's defence budget for initial design and research work. Seoul has also formally notified the International Atomic Energy Agency of its intention to begin consultations related to the programme.Defence minister nominee Kang Shin-chul has described nuclear-powered submarines as providing a “persistent and stealthy deterrent” against North Korea. He has also highlighted their potential role in protecting sea lanes and their broader implications for South Korea's defence, nuclear energy and shipbuilding industries.US Congress examines risksThe programme is also drawing greater scrutiny in Washington.The US Senate Armed Services Committee has called for an assessment of how South Korea's nuclear-powered submarine programme could affect Indo-Pacific security, proliferation risks and costs, as well as the potential scope of future bilateral cooperation.For Seoul, the challenge will be to demonstrate that the submarines are not simply an expensive response to prestige or military competition, but a capability with a clearly defined strategic purpose.If the vessels are initially designed to counter North Korean submarine threats but retain the endurance and operational flexibility to protect maritime trade and support allied missions farther afield, their role could gradually expand from a peninsula-focused deterrent into a broader Indo-Pacific undersea capability.

articles.title: Will record donations to Reform be a moment of political change?
articles.summary: Andy Burnham is likely to face fresh pressure to further change the rules on party donations, writes Jack Fenwick.
articles.body:
When news of Reform UK's two record-breaking £36m donations emerged this weekend, it felt as if Nigel Farage's inner circle was attempting a fightback.

The last few months have proved difficult for the party, with a dip in the polls, a spike in infighting and a series of questions about money that simply won't go away.

In contrast, the mood within the ranks of Labour and the Conservatives has been fairly chipper.

Most Labour MPs feel Andy Burnham has got off to an impressive start as prime minister, while many Conservatives are feeling confident about Kemi Badenoch's recent reshuffle of her top team.

But Reform has been quietly - and as of this weekend rather loudly - building a formidable war chest.

Even before these two mega donations, Reform had raised £30.5m since the start of the year, more than double their nearest rivals.

This extra £72m takes them into uncharted financial territory, which the party says will be used to hire the brightest policy minds, as well as up to 400 campaign managers in every target seat around the country.

In a world of fractured politics, when seats can be won on increasingly smaller percentages of the vote, having a ground campaign that is effective at getting out the core voter base could become increasingly important.

Some in Westminster have been less than convinced by Burnham's insistence that he won't call an early general election.

It might be tempting for the prime minister to go to the polls before Farage has had time to splash the cash on a shiny new party machine.

Some Labour MPs think that could factor into his thinking, but one Number 10 source insisted Reform's extra cash does not make an early election any more likely.

Burnham is now likely to come under increasing pressure to further change the rules on party donations.

There has been much talk about whether that could impact the donations to Reform by cryptocurrency billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, but when interviewed by the BBC, Angela Rayner refused to say whether the two would be caught up in the rule changes.

The Liberal Democrats and Greens have also called for a cap for people based in Britain too, to prevent future mega donations.

Burnham has indicated that he's open to having that conversation, but chose not to support an effort by some Labour MPs earlier this month to tighten the rules.

Rayner confirmed this morning that it was still something being considered by ministers.

The Electoral Commission is looking at what more should be done in this area and the calls from within Labour for further change will now grow stronger.

Government sources insist this weekend's donations are not being viewed inside Downing Street as a game-changing moment in this debate.

But people across the political spectrum are now asking whether this massive injection of money will be remembered as a key moment when politics in this country changed.

articles.title: Fall makes its move on the Midwest and Northeast this week
articles.summary: A blast of fall-like weather is coming to the Midwest and Northeast early this week as summer’s grip begins to loosen across the country.
articles.body: A blast of fall-like weather is coming to the Midwest and Northeast early this week as summer’s grip begins to loosen across the country. A pool of cold, dry air pushed into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest Saturday night and will sweep through Chicago, Detroit and the rest of the Midwest this evening through Monday morning, reaching the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic by Tuesday morning. 🍂 Get your local forecast from the CNN Weather app Temperatures dip into the 50s overnight, bottoming out in the 40s across the interior Northeast and Upper Midwest. That cold air will stick around during the day and limit the afternoon warmup, holding high temperatures to the mid-70s across the regions. Chicago will stay in the 70s today, dropping to the upper 50s Monday night as the cold air pushes on. New York City will follow, falling to 60 degrees overnight Monday and barely climbing back into the 70s on Tuesday. Boston and Providence will be even cooler, in 50s overnight and staying below 70 degrees through Wednesday morning. The cooldown is accompanied by a sharp drop in humidity — especially along the East Coast as cool, dry air pushes south into the Mid-Atlantic and lands on the eastern side of the Appalachians. The mountains will help lock the cold air in place through a process called cold air damming. Cold air is too dense to climb west back over the mountains, which act like a dam in a river, so it piles up against the eastern side of the slopes. The South and central US will stay locked in the heat that’s gripped both regions for weeks, with highs still reaching into the 90s and 100s. The Southeast likely won’t get its first real taste of fall weather until later in the week, possibly stretching into next week. But cold outbreaks like this one will become more common as the Northern Hemisphere tips into the darker half of the year. Major cities including Chicago, Minneapolis, New York, Washington DC, and Boston have all already lost upwards of two hours of daylight since the summer solstice, the longest day of the year. They are now losing daylight at close to their fastest pace of the year, over 17 minutes per week. The longer nighttime hours give the atmosphere more time each day to cool down, allowing cold air masses to expand across North America.

articles.title: Russian drone strike near Polish border in Ukraine, forcing temporary closure
articles.summary: A Russian drone struck near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the small town of Yahodyn overnight, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday.
articles.body: KYIV — A Russian drone struck near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the small town of Yahodyn overnight, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday. The minister corrected his earlier statement saying the drone struck on the border crossing at Yahodyn. “Russia’s barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders,” Sybiha said on X. “This is Putin’s terror “knocking” directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” he added. Polish border guard spokeswoman told Reuters that the site of the attack was less than a mile from the Polish border, and the border crossing was temporarily closed during the attack. In a separate statement, Ukrainian Railways, Ukrzaliznytsia, said that in another region bordering Poland, Volyn, a drone attacked the locomotive of a passenger train just 1.2 miles from the Polish border. The company said no one was injured. Ukraine operates several border crossings with Poland, through which a significant proportion of the military and humanitarian aid from its allies is delivered to the country.

articles.title: In 1936, Memphis built Overton Park Shell for $14,000; 18 years later Elvis played his first paid concert there, and 90 years on the stage is still hosting shows
articles.summary: US News: A historic open-air stage in Memphis, Tennessee, built for just $14,000 during the Great Depression, is celebrating nine decades of live music with a .
articles.body: A historic open-air stage in Memphis, Tennessee, built for just $14,000 during the Great Depression, is celebrating nine decades of live music with a major series of public concerts. The Overton Park Shell, built in 1936 as a Works Progress Administration project, became internationally known 18 years later when 19-year-old Elvis Presley performed his first paid professional show on its stage. Today, 90 years after its first performance, the iconic venue remains an active community music centre, hosting dozens of free and ticketed concerts each season. The milestone was reported by Memphis television station Action News 5, along with official updates published on the Overton Park Shell digital archive platform.From Depression-era construction to rock and roll historyDesigned by architect Max Furbringer and based on the famous Hollywood Bowl, the acoustic band shell was built with joint funding from the City of Memphis and the federal government. When it opened in September 1936, construction had cost about $14,000. The venue was designed as an affordable outdoor performance space for the wider public. On 30 July 1954, the venue became part of modern music history. A young Elvis Presley appeared on the stage as an opening act for country musician Slim Whitman. Original promotional posters listed him as "Elvis Pressley". The performance was Presley's first advertised, paid professional appearance after the release of his debut Sun Records single, "That's All Right". According to historical records on the Overton Park Shell portal, Presley's energetic movements on the wooden stage drew a strong reaction from the audience. The performance helped establish a new style of live rock and roll shows that would later spread around the world. Over the following decades, the stage welcomed a wide range of musicians, including country pioneer Johnny Cash, blues legend Furry Lewis, classical orchestras, and modern indie bands. This helped establish the shell as one of the most historically important open-air music venues in the United States.Community fight saves venue from demolitionDespite its history, the venue faced serious neglect and possible demolition in the late 20th century. In the mid-1980s, commercial redevelopment plans proposed replacing the amphitheatre with a parking lot. Local activists and arts supporters formed Save Our Shell, a grassroots group that stopped the demolition plans and helped secure municipal protection for the site. A later major restoration project was carried out with the Levitt Foundation. The venue was then known as the Levitt Shell for more than a decade. In 2022, the non-profit board that operates the venue officially restored its original historical name, the Overton Park Shell, while also expanding its work to include mobile outreach programmes. Action News 5 reported that the non-profit organisation running the stage now depends on corporate sponsorships, private donations and partnerships with the city to maintain the historic structure while keeping free public access to the arts.90 years of performances marked with major lineupTo celebrate its 90th anniversary season, Overton Park Shell management announced an expanded concert programme featuring a mix of local, national and international artists. The programme includes the Shell Yeah! Benefit Concert Series as well as the long-running Free Concert Series, which provides accessible music programmes to tens of thousands of visitors each year. According to schedules published on the official Overton Park Shell platform, the anniversary events cover genres from Delta blues and soul to modern alternative rock and brass bands. The varied programme reflects the long and diverse musical history of Memphis. Along with concerts at the main amphitheatre in Overton Park, the organisation has expanded its reach through the "Shell on Wheels" initiative. The mobile programme uses a specially designed vehicle to take live music, sound equipment and staging directly to underserved neighbourhoods across Memphis and Shelby County. Leaders of the non-profit organisation said in updates provided to Action News 5 that the 90-year milestone shows the lasting importance of public cultural spaces. As the autumn season continues, the open-air stage remains an important part of the Memphis music community, operating on the same ground where a young truck driver once helped change the course of popular music.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Henry Xie: The 17-year-old Portland student whose method made smaller AI models more empathetic in at least 90% of tests
articles.summary: US News: A 17-year-old student from Portland, Oregon, has developed a two-step training method that helps small artificial intelligence models copy the empathe.
articles.body: A 17-year-old student from Portland, Oregon, has developed a two-step training method that helps small artificial intelligence models copy the empathetic communication style of much larger systems. The method achieved higher empathy ratings in at least 90 per cent of comparison tests. Henry Xie, a senior at Westview High School in Portland, created the computer science project "Distilling Empathy From Large Language Models" for the Regeneron Science Talent Search, the leading science and mathematics competition for high school seniors in the United States. Official information published by the Society for Science confirmed that Xie was named a national finalist and received a $25,000 award for his research into ethical artificial intelligence. Xie's method tackles a key problem in current AI technology. Large language models (LLMs) with billions of parameters, such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, can produce detailed and emotionally supportive responses. However, they need large amounts of computing power, costly server systems and a constant internet connection. Small language models (SLMs), on the other hand, can run directly on devices such as smartphones, laptops and wearable technology. They do not need the same level of server support and can respond with low delay. However, these smaller models have traditionally struggled to understand emotional details and often produce mechanical or detached replies.A two-step framework for teaching empathyTo close this gap, Xie created a two-step training framework that transfers empathetic reasoning from large AI systems to smaller models without increasing their memory or processing requirements. During the first training stage, Xie collected published examples of empathetic conversations produced by LLMs such as ChatGPT and Gemini. He based the data on established psychological ideas about communication and supportive listening. He then used these examples to train small language models and teach them basic patterns for using empathetic language. In the second stage, Xie added specific prompts that encouraged the smaller models to assess their own possible responses. By comparing stronger empathetic answers with weaker or dismissive ones, the models learned to choose responses that better recognised and responded to people's emotional states. Evaluation results published by the Society for Science show that when the responses were assessed using LLMs, the small models trained with Xie's method were rated as more empathetic than basic, untrained SLMs in at least 90 per cent of test situations.Making human-focused AI available on personal devicesAlongside his research, Xie has also worked on technology access and AI ethics in his local community. The son of Fei Xie and Huaiyu Liu, he is president of the computer science club and captain of the varsity swim team at Westview High School. Xie is also a three-time semifinalist in the CyberPatriot National Youth Cyber Defense Competition, one of the main youth cybersecurity competitions in the United States, according to background information. Xie also co-founded Youth for Empathetic AI, a student-led non-profit group that connects high school researchers with academic mentors. The organisation aims to encourage the development of human-focused artificial intelligence and greater involvement by young people in discussions about AI governance."Corals in Hawaii grow so, so slowly that it may take hundreds of years to recover from an event like that," noted researchers in related computer science literature examining ethical models, emphasizing that foundational training approaches determine long-term AI behavior. By helping small language models produce empathetic responses directly on personal devices, Xie's research shows that advanced conversational features could work locally without sending sensitive user information to cloud servers. The findings could provide a way to add more emotionally aware AI features to everyday mobile apps, wellness tools and accessible consumer devices.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ​Bangsamoro’s parliamentary election is a turning point
articles.summary: It’s a milestone of the self-determination fight in this region of the Philippines. It must be kept peaceful and fair.
articles.body:
On Monday, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the Philippines will hold its first parliamentary election since it was established in 2018. The vote will officially mark the end of the transition period under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), an interim regional government appointed in 2019.

The election is a significant milestone in the Bangsamoro struggle. It is the outcome of decades of armed conflict and negotiations between the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and the government of the Philippines.

The vote will test the Philippine government’s commitment to the peace process and the MILF’s commitment to the democratic process.

BARMM is located on Mindanao, the second-largest island in the Philippine Archipelago, and it covers roughly the territories inhabited by the Moro people, a native Muslim-majority group. For centuries, the Moro enjoyed self-governance in independent states and resisted Spanish colonialism. Following the Philippines’s independence in 1946, they continued their struggle for self-determination.

In 1989, the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) was created by Manila to give some devolved rights to the Moro. However, ARMM largely failed to address local grievances and demands due to its weak structural power. It was given limited autonomy in political and fiscal decision-making, but it did not manage to improve socioeconomic conditions in the region. The MILF continued the armed struggle.

In 2012, President Benigno Aquino III recognised the ARMM as a “failed experiment”. Under his administration, the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro was signed between the government and the MILF, paving the way for a new political entity.

Six years later, under President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, the Organic Law for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was promulgated. This legislation granted the region greater fiscal autonomy, a regional government, a parliament, and a justice system.

Then the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro was concluded to outline the mechanism of transition from ARMM to BARMM and set up the MILF-dominated BTA to lead it. All of this is culminating in the parliamentary election, which will determine the makeup of the region’s first legislative body.

The vote comes at a time of heightened tensions in BARMM and internal divisions within the MILF. Two camps have emerged within the movement – one loyal to MILF Chair Al Haj Murad Ebrahim and another supporting Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua.

Last month, Macacua joined the newly formed Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), which will compete in the elections against the MILF’s political wing, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP). Shortly after, his convoy was attacked, but he survived unscathed.

In early September, Macacua and 40 commanders were dismissed from the MILF’s military wing for alleged insubordination.

These tensions have prompted increased public anxiety about possible post-election unrest. There are other factors that could overshadow the vote.

In past elections, vote-buying was widespread, election-related violence was rampant, and electoral fraud and manipulation were pervasive. If these practices repeat at a large scale, the electoral outcome may not necessarily provide a straightforward measure of the will of Bangsamoro’s people. It may also not be an accurate reflection of whether they are satisfied with the transitional government or not.

The MILF presents itself as a champion of moral governance. If it is to retain this label, it should not give in to widespread vote-buying and electoral manipulation. It should also not let internal rivalries turn violent.

But there are already some alarming signs. Prominent MILF figures have conveyed that if the UBJP, the front’s political wing, sees manipulation and fraud, its members are ready to fight. They have also suggested that since the MILF led the transition, it should remain in power. On social media, some citizens have condemned the MILF camp’s threats, calling such tactics un-Islamic.

Before the vote, Manila has deployed military forces in key areas. This has heightened people’s fears that fighting with the MILF may erupt. The tense situation might lead to a low voter turnout.

Under these circumstances, the future of the Bangsamoro is riddled with uncertainties.

Whatever happens in the election, we must remember that the future of BARMM is a shared responsibility. The Philippine government and the Bangsamoro parties are duty-bound to honour the peace agreement. In addition, the people must exercise their civic rights and responsibilities to help sustain the peace achieved after a long and painful armed conflict and to move toward a prosperous Bangsamoro land.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Maya refutes illness claims, appears before media to dispel doubts
articles.summary: Mayawati dismisses illness rumours, appears before media; criticises expelled nephew Akash Anand, says he’s influenced by father-in-law Ashok Siddharth.
articles.body: Lucknow: Bahujan Samaj Party national president Mayawati on Sunday said that recently expelled functionaries are spreading propaganda that she is unwell, and therefore, communicating even major decisions through social media.Mayawati said she was appearing before media persons to dispel doubts about her health and said that she was fine and actively engaged in party work.Mayawati cited a late-night call to her office by nephew Akash Anand as evidence that such claims were being circulated. "Around 10 pm on Saturday, Akash called at my Lucknow office and asked party in charge Alok Kumar, who was present there, whether I am unwell and how is my health. Alok Kumar told him that I was fine and occupied with organisational work,” she said.Mayawati said she was not sure whether Akash’s intention was right or wrong, but questioned why did he say that she should not be informed about the call. Mayawati claimed that Akash was not using his own sense of judgment and was acting on the advice of Ashok Siddharth, his father-in-law.Akash Anand, elder son of Mayawati’s brother Anand Kumar, had been serving as the party’s national convener until Mayawati relieved him of all responsibilities on Thursday. She later removed him from the party, citing that he was “strongly attached” to Siddharth. Siddharth has since announced his retirement from politics, as Mayawati had demanded.Mayawati also reiterated that Akash Anand, his younger brother Ishan Anand, and future generations of the family would not hold posts in the party. She announced organisational changes linked to the party’s three-sector structure created at the all-India BSP meeting in Lucknow on Sept 3 to strengthen the organisation.Under the sector plan, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand form the first sector, while the remaining states are grouped into sectors two and three. Mayawati directly supervises the first sector. Ishan Anand had earlier been appointed chief central sector in charge, with office-bearers reporting to him. articles.title: No bin collections prompt demand for Flintshire council tax rebate
articles.summary: Nathan Long has been living on a housing estate for six months without bin collections.
articles.body:
A resident who has not had a bin collection for six months since moving on to a new-build estate is seeking a 100% council tax rebate as compensation.

Bins finally arrived on Hawthorn Meadows in Buckley, Flintshire, last month but Nathan Long and 60 other households can still only watch as refuse workers collect rubbish or recyclables from a nearby street.

Long said he wanted a rebate as he had been required to pay council tax since moving in and despite disposing of rubbish in skips provided by the estate developer.

The council said it was "working to resolve the situation" but a "multi-step setup process must occur" before new waste and recycling collection services are set up.

"It feels like we are not getting anywhere," said Long.

"We complain and we get responses that in part pass the buck on to others and in part pledge to do something about the problem.

"Meanwhile, we are sitting here watching bin crews collecting rubbish from across the road and wondering if they will ever come to us."

Mr Long is waiting to hear from the local authority about his request for a council tax rebate.

He added: "When we received our bins we thought that was the signal.

"But another month has passed and still nothing.

"At one point I went to lodge a formal complaint about the situation and was told I couldn't as technically we hadn't missed a collection."

Katie Wilby, council chief officer for streetscene and transportation, said: "While we normally expect developers to arrange these services before residents move in, we are currently working to resolve the situation for the occupied properties.

"A council officer will visit the site to confirm occupancy, perform safety checks, and integrate eligible homes into the collection system as quickly as possible."

Castle Green Homes said it would continue to provide skips for residents at its own cost until the matter is resolved.

articles.title: Kyrsten Sinema questions whether moderates still have a place in the Democratic Party
articles.summary: Kyrsten Sinema says Democratic Party leaders made "clear" they didn't want her there, raising questions about whether moderates still have a place.
articles.body: Former Arizona Sen. Kyrsten Sinema questioned whether there is still room for moderates in the Democratic Party, saying it was made "clear" they didn’t want her there before she abandoned her Democratic affiliation and became an independent. "The reason I left was because the party had decided they wanted to pursue a track of short-term gain and really sacrificing kind of longer-term issues around democracy, like the filibuster," she said Saturday on "My View with Lara Trump." "And they very much made it clear that they didn't really want me there. And, so, I left, which made me happy, and I think made them happy. "But I'm not sure that there's more room for others who are moderate or conservatives left there. ... That's unfortunate because the majority of Americans actually live in that moderate or fiscally conservative middle." SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' Sinema, who was elected to both the House and Senate as a Democrat before becoming an independent, said she left the party after Democrats pursued what she characterized as immediate political gains at the expense of longer-term institutional concerns, specifically citing the filibuster. She also contrasted the party she joined with the growing Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) movement, which she said is rooted in principles that do not reflect the "historic Democratic Party." WISCONSIN DEMOCRATIC CANDIDATE SAYS HER PARTY 'LEFT BEHIND' RURAL AMERICA Sinema said when she entered Congress in 2012, she was a "blue dog," a coalition she described as fiscally conservative and socially moderate. There were a lot more traditional liberal Democrats at that time, she said, stating that the DSA is something else entirely. "It's really rooted in tenets of socialism, which is not reflective of the historic Democratic Party. So, it's hard to tell whether it's a hijacking or whether it is actually the movement of the voters' opinions," she said. Sinema added that primary elections tend to reflect the extreme ends of both parties, so it is too soon to tell whether the broader Democratic base is actually on board with the DSA. articles.title: Since 2000, Marc Benioff and his wife bought more than 600 acres in Hawaii worth nearly $100 million; they later donated 440 acres for affordable housing, starting with 43 homes
articles.summary: US News: Since 2000, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and his wife, Lynne Benioff, have bought more than 600 acres of land in Hawaii worth nearly $100 million. Much.
articles.body: Since 2000, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and his wife, Lynne Benioff, have bought more than 600 acres of land in Hawaii worth nearly $100 million. Much of the land is in and around Waimea, a rural agricultural town on Hawaii’s Big IslandThe land buying increased after 2020, when the couple began purchasing residential, commercial and agricultural properties in Waimea. KQED found that Benioff had bought at least 38 parcels through six anonymous limited liability companies, or LLCs, and one nonprofit. The properties included more than 580 acres in Waimea and about 25 acres at beach resorts.The purchases attracted attention because Waimea has a close-knit community and a large Native Hawaiian population. Residents worried that wealthy buyers purchasing large amounts of land could increase competition for property and make it harder for local people to afford homes.The uncertainty also led to speculation about Benioff’s plans. Some residents believed he could be preparing a Salesforce facility or bringing engineers to the area, while others thought the purchases were connected to his charitable work. Benioff later rejected the idea of a Salesforce facility in Hawaii.Land donated for affordable housingA major part of the land purchases later became connected to affordable housing. Benioff and his wife donated 282 acres to the Hawaii Island Community Development Corp. (HICDC), an organisation that develops affordable housing on the Big Island.In June 2024, they donated another 158 acres to the organisation for the same purpose. The two donations brought their total contribution to 440 acres.The land is part of the Ouli Project in Waimea. The project will begin with 43 self-help affordable housing units and will include single-family homes, parks and community spaces.HICDC Executive Director Keith Kato said the project would help meet the need for affordable housing on Hawaii Island.“Our goal is to move quickly as affordable housing is needed today for low to moderate-income residents on Hawaii Island,” Kato said. “Without the Benioffs’ donations, none of this would be possible today.”The Benioffs also said they were pleased that HICDC could use the land to address the housing need. “We are so pleased that HICDC is able to use this land to support this important need,” they said in a statement.Why the purchases raised concernsBenioff had been buying property in Hawaii for years, but his focus changed after the pandemic began. During the first 15 years of his land purchases, he mainly bought beach resort properties. From 2020 onwards, he bought 22 parcels in and around Waimea.Some purchases were made for more than the current market value, according to KQED’s review of public records. One example was the property occupied by Mamane Bakery, a longtime local business that closed after Benioff bought the land.Residents said they were concerned about the effect of such purchases on housing costs. Hawaii was already facing affordability problems, while property prices in Waimea had increased sharply.KQED reported that median home prices in Waimea topped $1 million in January, 87% higher than before the pandemic. Across Hawaii, median home prices had risen by at least 22% from pre-pandemic levels, according to Redfin.State Senator Tim Richards said the pandemic brought an influx of people from the mainland who wanted to move to Hawaii.“We saw an influx of people coming from the mainland who wanted to get someplace that was, I guess, more isolated,” Richards said. “We saw a huge uptick of house sales and huge uptick of median price. … And that poses a problem.”“What young couple can afford that? Seriously. The answer is nobody,” he added.Not all the land was for philanthropyThe affordable housing donation was only part of Benioff’s Hawaii land holdings. KQED found that 11 of his 38 parcels were connected to philanthropy. These included land for the Ouli project and five residential properties donated to a private school in Waimea in 2022. Another 158-acre parcel next to Ouli was also planned for philanthropic use.However, 24 of the 38 parcels, covering about 165 acres, were set aside for Benioff and his family members. These included a private ranch with 10 horses and homes in Waimea and near the beach.Benioff said the properties were not being bought for Salesforce. He also rejected comparisons with other technology billionaires who have purchased large amounts of land in Hawaii.“Our philosophy has always been different, which is that we’re really only here to have a home for our family and then to give,” he said. “We don’t have outsized properties. We have basically enough for ourselves.” He also said he was not planning a bunker, adding, “I’m not a prepper.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Centre-left opposition bloc leads in Swedish vote, poll shows
articles.summary: Exit polls show Sweden’s centre-left parties with an early ⁠lead of 51.3 percent in general election.
articles.body:
Sweden’s centre-left opposition was projected to win 51.3 percent of the vote, ahead of the right-wing bloc’s 46.8 percent, according to an exit poll by public broadcaster SVT.

Voting in Sweden’s election ⁠ended at ⁠18:00 GMT on Sunday, ⁠and official counting is under way. Early results were expected from the Swedish Election Authority within hours.

A separate election-day poll conducted ⁠by broadcaster TV4 also showed the centre-left in the lead.

Swedish exit polls, while often indicative of the outcome, have not always proven accurate. In 2022, for example, a poll projected that Magdalena Andersson’s centre-left bloc would prevail, but the election was ultimately won by a right-wing coalition headed by Ulf Kristersson, Sweden’s current prime minister.

Earlier in this campaign, Sweden’s left-wing bloc appeared headed for a comfortable victory over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the nationalist Sweden Democrats. But the race tightened steadily in the final weeks of the race, turning what had looked like a relatively predictable election into a much closer contest.

Earlier in the year, polls had given the opposition bloc led by Andersson’s Social Democrats a lead of about 10 percentage points. By the final weeks of the campaign, that advantage had collapsed to just two to three points.

A victory for Andersson would provide some respite for left-leaning parties across Europe, where right-wing and far-right parties have been gaining ground. Just last week, Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44 percent of the vote in a key state election , putting a far-right party within reach of power at state level in Germany for the first time since World War II.

If the early exit polls are wrong, however, Sweden’s election could instead bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into government for the first time. A party with roots in the neo-Nazi movement, it won 20.5 percent of the vote in the 2022 election, becoming the largest party on the right and a crucial source of parliamentary support for Kristersson’s minority government.

Until now, however, the Sweden Democrats have remained outside government. Kristersson announced in April that his conservative Moderates would be prepared to bring the party into a governing coalition if the right secured a majority, which would give the Sweden Democrats cabinet positions for the first time.

But if the exit-poll lead is confirmed, the Sweden Democrats would be less likely to enter government.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk statue defaced with red paint, Jesus crossed out days after 1-year mark of assassination
articles.summary: Red paint was smeared across the Charlie Kirk statue at Turning Point USA's Phoenix headquarters, with a Christian tribute defaced days after unveiling.
articles.body: Vandals smeared bright red paint across a newly unveiled statue of Charlie Kirk and defaced a Christian tribute outside Turning Point USA’s Phoenix headquarters early Sunday, just three days after the memorial was installed. Images from the headquarters show red paint streaked across the eight-foot statue’s face and neck, with a crude frowning face drawn across its chest. A sign at the base of the statue bearing Kirk’s image and the words "Jesus defeated death so you can live" was also targeted. The word "Jesus" and an image of a cross appeared to be crossed out, while "Satan" was apparently scrawled across the display. REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR Kirk's widow, Erika, who now serves as Turning Point USA CEO, responded with a defiant vow to rebuild, saying the vandals would not erase her husband’s legacy or silence Christians. "Charlie once said we should be building two statues for every statue that they tear down," Erika Kirk wrote, adding that her husband’s instinct was always to create rather than destroy. She said the bullet that killed her husband only amplified his voice and predicted the spray paint would spread his legacy even further. She also vowed to restore the statue, replace Jesus Christ’s name on the damaged sign and continue the movement her husband built. "God will not be mocked," Erika Kirk wrote. Phoenix police confirmed to Fox News Digital that the department began receiving calls around 8:09 a.m. reporting vandalism to a memorial in the area of 4900 East Beverly Road. "Officers have responded to the location, and the incident is under investigation," police said. No arrests or suspect descriptions had been announced as of Sunday afternoon. "This morning we woke up to radical criminals vandalizing our headquarters," Turning Point USA Chief Operating Officer Tyler Bowyer wrote on social media. "Crossing over Charlie’s face, scratching out Jesus and the Cross and spraying red paint on his neck. "This isn’t the country we want to live in," Bowyer added. "Arizona is not Gotham." INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES Bowyer, who went to the headquarters as police investigated, said TPUSA was prepared to clean the memorial as soon as authorities released the scene. "God bless the police as they investigate the violent thugs who did this," Bowyer wrote. TPUSA also released video showing the damage and encouraged its supporters to vote ahead of the midterm elections. "Hate cannot win," the organization wrote. "The radical Left is showing up to vote. What are you doing to save the country from this?" In a follow-up statement, TPUSA said it would restore the statue and replace the damaged signs while reviewing footage of the incident and working with law enforcement to identify those responsible. "Vandalism like this is not funny, it’s diabolical," the organization wrote. "The incident happened in the middle of the night because evil never sleeps." TPUSA said the vandals went beyond spraying Kirk’s face and neck with red paint, accusing them of making an "intentional decision" to cross out Jesus’ name on the nearby sign. The organization ended its response by quoting John 15:18: "If the world hates you, keep in mind that it hated me first." The vandalism struck only days after TPUSA unveiled the bronze statue Thursday to mark one year since Kirk was assassinated while speaking at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. CHARLIE KIRK STATUE BOUND FOR NY'S TIMES SQUARE AS SCULPTOR DEFIES THREATS AHEAD OF UNVEILING The statue depicts Kirk wearing his signature "Freedom" T-shirt and cross necklace. Those who knew him said the sculpture captured details down to his wedding ring, according to FOX 10 Phoenix. Turning Point USA commissioned Utah artist Quintin McCann to create the memorial after he began working on a portrait of Kirk the evening the conservative activist was killed, according to the outlet. ITALIAN ARTIST UNVEILS CHARLIE KIRK MEMORIAL STATUE HE PLANS TO FEATURE AT TIMES SQUARE "Someone’s death, who I’ve never met, has never impacted me so much," McCann told FOX 10. "And I’m sure many people can agree. And I just stayed at work that evening and just started sculpting his portrait." The statue was initially placed outside TPUSA’s headquarters near 48th Street and Beverly Road but was expected to be moved indoors for security reasons by the end of the week, the outlet reported. REPUBLICAN CONVENTION ATTENDEES SHARE HEARTFELT TRIBUTES TO LATE CHARLIE KIRK ON ASSASSINATION ANNIVERSARY Conservative voices erupted over the attack, condemning the vandalism as another assault on Kirk’s family, friends and legacy. "Truly abhorrent," Rep. Abe Hamadeh, R-Ariz., wrote on X. "The Charlie Kirk statue that was just unveiled at Turning Point’s HQ was vandalized overnight with red paint. "The young people who work at Turning Point don’t deserve this, Charlie’s family doesn’t deserve this, his friends don’t deserve this," Hamadeh added. "The left is intolerant and militant. Evil exists and must be confronted continuously." Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., was equally blunt. "This is absolute evil," Biggs wrote. Conservative commentator Benny Johnson accused the vandals of trying to intimidate Kirk’s supporters. "These people are incapable of building anything, all they know is destruction," Johnson wrote. "Keep these demons out of power." TPUSA contributor Alex Clark said seeing the damage brought her to tears before issuing a dire warning to conservative voters. "The left wants to tap dance in your blood and throw confetti at your gravestone," Clark wrote. "Vote red in midterms like your life depends on it because it actually does as a conservative." Turning Point USA Chief of Staff Mikey McCoy urged conservatives to answer the vandalism with faith, invoking Kirk’s willingness to return to hostile campuses and the biblical examples of Stephen and Christ praying for those who persecuted them. "Then I can surrender all the anger, and pure disgust that I feel at seeing this to a just and holy God," McCoy wrote, saying he would pray instead for the repentance and salvation of those responsible. "Lord, help our Country," he added. "Open their eyes. Break their hearts. Save them." Bowyer also blasted Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, accusing her of failing to pursue bipartisanship after Kirk’s killing and pointing to her veto of legislation that would have named Loop 202 in Kirk’s honor. Hobbs said in her March veto letter that she condemned political violence but argued highway-naming decisions should remain nonpartisan and be handled by the state board responsible for such designations. Kirk was 31 when he was shot and killed during a TPUSA event at Utah Valley University. Tyler Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges in Kirk’s death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Erika Kirk took over as CEO of Turning Point USA after her husband’s assassination. The conservative organization he co-founded in 2012 has continued expanding its network of high school and college chapters since his death. articles.title: Left-wing bloc leads Swedish vote after far-right lose support, exit polls say
articles.summary: Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson may return as prime minister - a job she held from 2021 to 2022.
articles.body:
The left-wing political bloc in Sweden is leading the race to form a new government, according to exit polls from Sunday's general election.

The four-party bloc was projected to get 51.3% of votes against 46.8% for the right, public broadcaster SVT and TV4 said.

If confimed, it will mean the Social Democrats' leader Magdalena Andersson will be Sweden's new prime minister - a job she held from 2021 to 2022.

Current conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has promised cabinet jobs for hard-right allies if he stays in charge.

Close race in Sweden as hard right eyes role in government

Kristersson has been supported in government by the hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), which have neo-Nazi roots.

Exit polls suggested the party which entered parliament in 2010 would lose support for the first time.

Sweden has two major political blocs featuring four parties on the right and four on the left - meaning coalition and minority governments are relatively common.

Andersson's party, the Social Democrats, have been a major force in Swedish politics since the end of World War Two.

But SD - founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s - had been shunned for years until 2022 when it became the country's second largest party after campaigning on violent crime and immigration.

After casting her vote on Sunday, Andersson laid out the choice facing the Swedish public: "Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats, something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of co-operation?"

Kristersson, for his part, said it was important he and his alliance were able to continue their work.

"I think there is a genuine enthusiasm for us being able to continue our important work," he said after casting his ballot in his home municipality of Strangnas.

National security, gang crime and welfare spending dominated the election campaign.

articles.title: In 1957, officials released one male and one female wild sheep on a remote Kerguelen island; 46 years later, their isolated population had higher genetic diversity
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A groundbreaking study reveals remarkable genetic diversity in the mouflon population on Haute Island, challenging traditional theories in population genetics and highlighting the impacts of natural selection and reproduction dynamics over nearly five decades.
articles.body: One male and one female yearling mouflon were released onto Haute Island of the Kerguelen archipelago in 1957, thus giving rise to the isolated population under study. To make that possible, a single yearling male and a single yearling female Corsican mouflon were brought from the Vincennes Zoo in Paris and released on Haute Island, a 6.5 square kilometre patch of land roughly 3,000 kilometres from Réunion, the departure point for supply ships serving the archipelago's research base at Port-aux-Français. No one involved at the time could have anticipated that this pair would later challenge a familiar assumption in population genetics.A single pair founds a population on one of the world's most isolated islandsHaute Island is located in the Kerguelen archipelago in the southern Indian Ocean and is an isolated French possession with a scientific station as its principal permanent facility. The mouflon population grew rapidly at first because there were no predators or migration, reaching an estimated 100 animals by the early 1970s and peaking at 700 in 1977. Cycles eventually occurred in the population, reaching peaks of more than 700 individuals followed by a sharp decline and further oscillations, with die-offs occurring every two to five years. By the time the biologists focused on this herd decades later, it had already become a wild herd consisting entirely of descendants of those two animals.Researchers trace genetic change across 46 yearsThis lengthy history meant that Haute Island was a unique biological laboratory for study purposes. Tissue samples taken from mouflon on Haute Island between 1957 and 2003 provided genetic data spanning 46 years from a population founded by very few animals. These samples were analyzed by Kaeuffer R., Coltman D.W., Chapuis J-L., Pontier D., and Réale D. in their article Unexpected heterozygosity in an island mouflon population founded by a single pair of individuals, in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. The researchers used 25 microsatellite markers to determine heterozygosity, which is a common measure of genetic diversity. According to the study, the founders of the population were only two individuals, a single male and female, in the year 1957; yet average heterozygosity levels were still very high, even surpassing Hardy-Weinberg expectations at some loci. By utilizing multilocus genotypes gathered between 1957 and 2003, the researchers propose that this is better explained by balancing selection or random retention, rather than genetic drift alone.Genetic diversity rises instead of falling, defying standard drift modelsThe predictions made by traditional population genetics were quite contrary to the results obtained by the researchers. Small founder groups should experience loss in genetic variability because each new generation receives only a random sample of the genes from the previous one. By contrast, the 2007 article showed that observed heterozygosity increased rather than decreased over the 46 years after introduction, and that it exceeded the levels predicted by neutral models and stochastic simulations. Selection was mentioned as one of the possible causes of such an observation, although some limitations were noted by the researchers in their models, such as generation overlap, population sizes and ascertainment bias.A follow-up study points to twinning and selectionA related study offered a possible clue to the unexpected genetic pattern. In Local effects of inbreeding on embryo number and consequences for genetic diversity in Kerguelen mouflon, published via the National Center for Biotechnology Information, Kaeuffer et al. examined the differences in the number of embryos among ewes of various degrees of multilocus heterozygosity. It has also been found that there is a very high twinning frequency of 33.8% in the Kerguelen mouflon, which is much higher than the frequency of 2.5-20.7% in European mouflons. Since such a high frequency existed even in the ancestral population, it seems likely that genes for twinning could have been present in the founder population.Unlike the traditional expectation that inbreeding could have a detrimental effect on reproductive success, the study showed that heterozygosity for three marker genes, namely, TEXAN4, DRBps and BM848, was significantly correlated with the number of embryos. However, the authors caution that the correlation does not mean a proportional increase in heterozygosity would produce a proportional increase in embryo number. The three SNPs TEXAN4, DRBps and BM848 were significantly linked to embryo count, even after correction for multiple tests, but the genes corresponding to the above association remain unknown. The authors suggested that twinning carries costs, including higher reproductive demands and increased mortality during the population's periodic declines. If the cost hypothesis is correct, selection could ultimately favor heterozygosity, or at least help maintain genetic diversity despite local genetic effects.Why a small island herd matters for conservation geneticsTaken together, the two studies suggest that genetic drift may not be the only evolutionary force shaping genetic diversity in this small isolated population, the researchers argue. Natural selection related to reproductive factors, and more specifically, twinning costs and benefits, might be offsetting some of the reduction in heterozygosity seen in neutral theory models. The longitudinal approach used in the Haute Island mouflon study is relatively uncommon in population genetics, where researchers often rely on comparisons among populations or sampling periods. In the case of the Kerguelen Archipelago, the founder effect alone does not determine a population's genetic future. Other factors also help maintain genetic diversity within a small population: generation overlap, uneven reproduction, population cycles, and natural selection.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Tom Homan confirmed officials are investigating allegations involving Rep. Ilhan Omar but declined to share specifics about possible immigration fraud.
articles.body: White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed on "The Sunday Briefing" that the Department of Homeland Security is looking into allegations involving Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., but would not disclose details about what he described as an "ongoing criminal investigation." Pressed on whether the federal government has evidence that Omar committed immigration or naturalization fraud, Homan declined to comment. "I know things are going on, but I can't give specifics of what's happening," Homan said. "If someone committed an immigration violation, if someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they're a congressman or not, no one's above the law. So, I'll leave it at that. We'll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, continue the investigation." FEDS SAY RAPE CONVICT LIED HIS WAY INTO US CITIZENSHIP BY HIDING SEX ASSAULTS When subsequently asked directly whether he was confirming an investigation involving Omar, Homan replied, "I'm confirming that ICE is, yeah — look, I said months ago that there's something that's been reported and needs to be looked at." Omar has long been dogged by allegations that she married a man that critics allege is her brother as part of an immigration scheme. Omar has repeatedly denied the allegation, and the claim has not been proven in public records. In December, she dismissed the claims as "bigoted lies," writing on social media that Trump was obsessed with her. Homan's comments follow Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin's appearance on a podcast, during which he said, "Something's going to happen. ... We know that she married her brother to try to bring him to the United States. We know he now lives in London. ILHAN OMAR LASHES OUT AT 'SICK' REPUBLICANS FOR INVESTIGATING HER ALLEGED MARRIAGE TO BROTHER "There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with. ... If we can prove it, that you shouldn't have been here in the first place, we will deport you." Homan did not disclose any information about possible evidence or charges. 'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP Vice President JD Vance said in May that the Justice Department was looking into whether Omar committed immigration fraud. articles.title: Chick-fil-A is one of America's toughest franchises, and the startup cost may shock you
articles.summary: Julian Good reveals Chick-fil-A's $10,000 franchise fee and the staggering odds facing 100,000 yearly applicants vying for roughly 200 spots.
articles.body: Chick-fil-A is one of America's toughest franchises to get, attracting thousands of hopeful applicants each year for a limited number of owner-operator opportunities. The fast-food chain's unique business model was recently highlighted by Julian Good, who owns a Chick-fil-A restaurant in St. Charles, Illinois, during an appearance on the "Founder Talk" podcast. "It's a $10,000 franchise fee. It's been the same for the last 50 years," Good said. CHICK-FIL-A COPYCAT RECIPE REVEALED AS CEO SHARES INGREDIENT THAT MAKES IT TASTE LIKE THE ORIGINAL About 100,000 people apply each year to become a Chick-fil-A owner-operator, with roughly 200 ultimately selected, Good explained. Applicants without Chick-fil-A experience often wait three to five years before receiving an opportunity, he added. Chick-fil-A describes its selection process as "highly competitive," saying it looks for leaders willing to devote their full time and best efforts to operating a restaurant, according to Chick-fil-A’s January 2024 post on its press room website. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER However, previous experience with the company isn't required. More than 25% of newly selected owner-operators had never worked at one of its restaurants or for the company before applying, according to Chick-fil-A. The company said operators also come from a wide range of professional backgrounds, including manufacturing, health care, education, law enforcement and retail. Unlike many franchise systems, Chick-fil-A owner-operators do not own the restaurant they operate, according to Franchise Business Review. Chick-fil-A retains ownership of the restaurant, equipment and, in most cases, the real estate, meaning operators do not build equity in the business or sell it when they retire. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Chick-fil-A said operators devote their time and energy to managing their restaurants, developing employees and serving their communities. Good said that's one of the biggest differences between Chick-fil-A and many competing franchise models. "When a Chick-fil-A operator retires, you can't pass it down to your kids. You don't sell the business or anything. It just goes back into the hands of Chick-fil-A," he said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Chick-fil-A's unique approach also extends to its operating schedule, with all of its restaurants closed on Sundays. The weekly tradition remains an important part of the company's culture, Good noted. "Just a way to glorify God and give back to the team and the community," he said. articles.title: US will scrap Irish whisky tariff, Trump says
articles.summary: The announcement comes several months after the US decreased the tariff by 5 percent.
articles.body:
While in Ireland attending a golf tournament at the golf course he owns in Doonbeg in County Clare, US President Donald Trump said the US will repeal a 10 percent tariff on Irish whisky, a duty that currently falls ⁠under those imposed on all European Union wine and spirit exports to the United States.

“Everybody’s been bugging me” to do it, the president said at a trophy ceremony. “And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off [Irish whisky].'”

Irish whisky producers have been navigating the tariffs levied by the Trump administration on European Union imports for over a year, as part of the administration’s broader trade and import clampdown.

Trump announced a zero-tariff policy for spirits from the United Kingdom in late April, removing duties on Scotch and Northern Irish whisky following a royal visit from the UK’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla.

“The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do, without hardly even asking!” Trump posted on social media at the time.

The Scotch Whisky Association said July 24 that the zero-tariff policy had come into effect, calling it “welcome news for businesses on both sides of the Atlantic” that would provide “greater confidence to invest, grow exports, and support jobs and communities”.

In May, the Irish Whiskey Association (IWA) also pressed for tariff elimination to shield US spirit portfolios and consumers from market volatility, while buttressing domestic companies handling Irish brands.

In July, the administration dropped an original 15 percent tariff to 10 percent.

The IWA welcomed the announcement and said it would continue to work with its EU and US counterparts to secure a return ‌to the zero-for-zero tariff arrangement for all drinks exports.

“Nothing exemplifies the US-Ireland trade relationship better than Irish Whiskey,” IWA Director Eoin O Caithain said in a statement, adding ‌that ‌the lobby group looked forward to seeing the announcement fully implemented.

Trump’s sudden announcement at the tournament’s close triggered a chorus of whistles and cheers from the crowd of spectators. Details on how soon the tariff would be lifted were not immediately available.

articles.title: In 1995, just 51 rare snakes survived on one tiny Caribbean island; 21 years later their population topped 1,100
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 1995, the Antiguan racer was perilously close to disappearing from the wild. Just 51 of these rare Caribbean snakes were estimated to survive, all .
articles.body: In 1995, the Antiguan racer was perilously close to disappearing from the wild. Just 51 of these rare Caribbean snakes were estimated to survive, all confined to tiny Great Bird Island off the coast of Antigua. The species had little room to recover. Yet what followed became an extraordinary conservation turnaround. Over the next 21 years, researchers and conservation groups removed invasive mammals, carefully moved snakes to other islands and monitored their progress. By 2016, the population had climbed to more than 1,100 individuals, showing how targeted conservation can pull a species back from the brink.Removing black rats doubled the rare snake populationAccording to the research published on ResearchGate titled ‘ Successful reintroduction of the Critically Endangered Antiguan racer Alsophis antiguae to offshore islands in Antigua, West Indies’, one of the ways was to remove Black rats from Great Bird Island. A consortium involving Antiguan and international conservation organisations carried out the eradication in 1995. The result was striking: the racer population promptly doubled, and within two years it had more than doubled from its original level.But protecting the surviving snakes on one small island was not considered enough. According to the study, the conservation team recognised that Great Bird Island had limited space and that further population growth would eventually be constrained. A 10-year plan was therefore developed to establish racers on other offshore islands, with an initial goal of increasing the global population to at least 500 individuals.86 rare snakes were moved to three islandsRabbit, Green and York were selected because they offered suitable habitat, prey and opportunities to control invasive mammals. Before they were released, conservationists had to remove rats and mongooses, since these animals could prey on the racers or reduce the lizards the snakes depend on.The first transfer took place in November 1999, when researchers moved 10 wild racers from Great Bird Island to Rabbit Island. Further releases followed on Green Island in 2002 and on York Island from 2008. Researchers eventually translocated 86 racers to the three islands between 1999 and 2012. According to the researchers, the released snakes adapted well, with no deaths recorded during the translocation or radiotelemetry studies.New generations showed the reintroduction was workingThe success of the transfers became clear when the relocated snakes began reproducing. According to the study, unmarked racers, meaning snakes that had not been part of the original translocated groups, were observed on all three reintroduction islands within three years of the first releases. This confirmed that the snakes were breeding and that new generations were becoming established away from their original stronghold.The researchers also found signs that the new islands could provide better conditions for growth. According to the study, translocated racers showed accelerated growth on Rabbit, Green and York islands, potentially because they faced less competition for resources than on the relatively crowded Great Bird Island. One female released on Green Island was recaptured seven years later in excellent condition, while the study also recorded that the oldest known racers reached at least 16 years of age.Rare snake population topped 1,100 by 2016The figures eventually transformed the story from one of near extinction into one of the Caribbean's notable reptile conservation successes. According to the researchers' estimates, the total Antiguan racer population peaked at 1,135 individuals in 2015 before dipping slightly to an estimated 1,108 in 2016. The four island populations together occupied about 63 hectares, compared with just 8.4 hectares on Great Bird Island in 1995.Field research, fundraising and a public education campaign were all important parts of the programme. Conservationists worked to change negative attitudes towards snakes, explaining that Antiguan racers are harmless and highlighting their environmental role. Yet the researchers warned that the species still depended on protection from invasive mammals and damaging development, while additional reintroduction sites would be needed to spread the risk. The result is remarkable: from an estimated 51 snakes on a tiny 8.4-hectare island in 1995 to more than 1,100 across four islands by 2016.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
